item.title: Binary GCD
item.description: Euclid’s algorithm is almost two and a half millennia old. The instruction that limits it is much younger. item.title: Prime Number Sieves
item.description: There are two superficially similar prime-number problems. To decide whether one 64-bit integer is prime, we use algorithms such as Miller–Rabin. To enumerate every prime up to a limit $N$, testing the numbers independently repeats almost all of the work. A sieve wins by turning divisibility into a streaming memory problem. This makes prime generation an unusually clear performance case study. The arithmetic is elementary; the important decisions are which candidates we store, where each crossing-off pass starts, whether the working set fits in cache, and whether an expression such as p * p is even defined for the requested limit.

item.title: Integer Factorization
item.description: Integer factorization has an unusual performance profile. Dividing a number by every possible candidate is slow because division is slow, but replacing division is only the beginning: for a hard 64-bit input, there are billions of candidates not worth trying in the first place. This case study starts with trial division and ends with Pollard–Brent rho, which finds a factor by turning a number-theoretic collision into a greatest common divisor. The final implementation is intended for machine-word integers.

item.title: Optimizing Logistic Regression
item.description: Logistic regression is a small model with an honest performance lesson. Its mathematics fits on a page, but the program contains several distinct kernels: a dot product or matrix multiplication, a nonlinear probability conversion, a loss reduction, and—during training—an optimizer that decides how many times those kernels run. Combining them into one benchmark makes it easy to optimize the wrong thing. For class prediction, the exponential may be unnecessary. For probability output, it is required and must be evaluated stably.

item.title: Big Integers and Karatsuba Multiplication
item.description: Machine integers have a useful property: their cost does not depend on their value. Arbitrary-precision integers give up that abstraction. Adding a thousand-limb number touches a thousand limbs; multiplying two of them creates a small algorithm-selection problem. This chapter builds a nonnegative big integer from first principles. We begin with a normalized limb representation and schoolbook multiplication, derive Karatsuba’s three-product identity, and add a crossover that preserves the fast base case for small and strongly unbalanced operands.

item.title: Fast Fourier Transform
item.description: The discrete Fourier transform is a dense matrix-vector multiplication with an extraordinary matrix. Its entries are powers of one complex root, and that algebraic repetition lets us reduce $n^2$ work to $n\log n$. The fast Fourier transform is therefore not one algorithm but a family of factorizations of the DFT. We will derive the radix-2 Cooley–Tukey transform, implement an in-place iterative C++20 core, use it for linear convolution, and then examine the parts hidden by big-O notation: permutation, twiddle generation, vectorization, inverse scaling, and floating-point error.

item.title: Number-Theoretic Transform
item.description: The fast Fourier transform computes convolution quickly by evaluating polynomials at complex roots of unity. Its arithmetic is approximate. If the coefficients are integers and an exact modular result is acceptable—or can later be reconstructed—the same butterfly can run in a finite field. This is the number-theoretic transform (NTT). It replaces complex multiplication with modular multiplication, floating-point error with algebraic preconditions, and unrestricted power-of-two lengths with lengths supported by the chosen prime.

item.title: Argmin with SIMD
item.description: Finding the minimum of an array is a reduction. Finding where that minimum occurs is a reduction carrying luggage: every candidate value brings an index with it. That extra word changes the optimization problem. A vector minimum combines eight 32-bit values with one AVX2 instruction, but a vector argmin must also decide which indices survive, define what happens on ties, and reduce eight (value, index) pairs at the end. The fastest-looking loop is often the one that quietly gets one of those details wrong.

item.title: Prefix Sum with SIMD
item.description: A reduction turns an array into one value. A prefix sum turns it into all the intermediate reductions: $$ b_i=\sum_{j=0}^{i}a_j. $$ This operation is also called an inclusive scan. It is easy to distribute across cores, but awkward inside one SIMD register: element $i$ depends on element $i-1$, while SIMD is most comfortable when lanes are independent. The way out is to shorten the dependency chain. We will compute a small scan inside each vector with logarithmically many shifts, repair the boundary between the two 128-bit halves of AVX2, and carry one scalar sum from vector to vector.

item.title: Reading Decimal Integers
item.description: Reading an integer is easy when it happens once. Reading a few gigabytes of them is a small systems problem disguised as elementary arithmetic. There are really three different jobs involved: obtaining bytes from a file or a socket, finding the boundaries of the next token, converting the digits inside that token to an integer. Formatted input functions do all three, together with locale handling and a fairly generous grammar.

item.title: Writing Decimal Integers
item.description: Converting an integer to decimal looks like parsing played backwards. At the level of arithmetic it almost is; at the level of performance it is not. While parsing, the next digit arrives in the order in which Horner’s rule needs it. While formatting, the easiest operation gives us the digits in reverse order: $$ d = x \bmod 10, \qquad x \leftarrow \left\lfloor x / 10 \right\rfloor. $$ The last decimal digit appears first, so we either write backwards into a temporary buffer or discover the digit count in advance.

item.title: Reading and Writing Floating-Point Numbers
item.description: Integer conversion is mostly arithmetic in base ten. Floating-point conversion is arithmetic plus a proof. Consider the text 0.1. Its value is exactly $1/10$, but no finite binary fraction equals $1/10$. A parser must choose the nearest representable binary value. A formatter then faces the reverse problem: it should print enough decimal digits to identify that value, but usually no more than necessary. Both directions must make the same choice at boundaries where two floating-point numbers are almost equally close.

item.title: String Searching
item.description: Finding a byte in memory is a reduction: compare many positions and return the first match. Finding a string is a filtering problem: reject almost every position cheaply, then verify the survivors. That distinction matters more than the catalog of classical algorithms. On ordinary text, a two-byte filter may eliminate hundreds of candidates with a few vector instructions. On repetitive input, the same filter may accept every position, and only a worst-case linear algorithm prevents quadratic behavior.

item.title: Sorting
item.description: “How fast can we sort?” is not one question. It is a suitcase full of them. Are the keys arbitrary objects or fixed-width integers? Are comparisons cheap? Must equal keys retain their input order? May the algorithm allocate another array? Is the input random, nearly sorted, reverse sorted, or mostly duplicates? item.title: Matrix Multiplication
item.description: Matrix multiplication is where several modest optimizations learn to cooperate. Change the loop order and memory becomes sequential. Block the loops and cache lines are reused. Keep a tile of the result in registers and loads are reused. Apply SIMD and one instruction updates eight cells. None of these ideas is sufficient alone; together they separate a textbook triple loop from a BLAS kernel. They also create plenty of places to cheat accidentally.
